blocks.name: Playground
blocks.heading: Welcome. This is your portfolio's first draft.
blocks.subheading: You are inside the real editor with a demo document. Edit anything, break anything. Nothing is saved, and a refresh resets it all. Five short steps and you will know the whole machine.
roles: you are in the right place

blocks.content:
Why use this?

Because a portfolio should not take a weekend. Three honest pitches:

  • Need it today. Tabs, blocks, and a design picker instead of a blank file, a real portfolio in one sitting.
  • No code required. But it can help you. Hosted accounts edit and publish entirely in the browser; developers can fork the repo and own every line.
  • One JSON document. Everything you build here, tabs, blocks, posts, theme, is a single portable file you can export anywhere.

How this tour works

Five tabs across the top, one idea each. You are on 1 · Start. The big button at the bottom of every step jumps you to the next, or click the tabs yourself. And remember: everything is editable right now. Press Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + E, open the editor, and poke the very words you are reading.

blocks.heading: Done here?

blocks.content:
Everything is a block

Hero, marquee, card grid, entry list, rich text, blog, custom HTML, your portfolio is a stack of blocks. Press Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + E and this hidden command can be changed later too. Press Edit and add one with the + buttons in the editor, drag them by the ⠿ handle, delete fearlessly: Ctrl/Cmd + Z undoes everything. This tab is just blocks, one after another.

Write like you mean it

The Posts button (top right, while editing) opens the post manager; every post opens in the full-screen writer at /write, with a borderless title, live formatting, and an editable publish date. Published posts flow into the blog block you saw in step 2. Drafts stay private until you flip them.

Site-wide settings, one panel

The Site button next to Posts holds the global knobs: skins (HUD / Notebook / Clean, also switchable top-right, live, for every visitor), accent color, global font, view scale, socials, and the footer. Try flipping the skin right now, the whole tour re-skins around you.

blocks.content:
Make it real

Two doors out of the playground, both starting from what you just learned:

  • The fork (Product B). Fork the repo, run it, and edit for real. Then publish by exporting the JSON and pasting it over content/portfolio.json in your fork. Git push, rebuild, live.
  • The hosted account (Product A). Sign up from the hub, onboard in two minutes, press Save. Your portfolio is at /u/your-name instantly, no rebuilds ever.

Both speak the same JSON, so you can jump between them whenever you like.

posts.title: Welcome to your portfolio
posts.content:
This whole site, tabs, blocks, cards, hero, blog, is one JSON document. What you are reading is the demo seed that ships with the repository, written to show off what the platform can do before you replace all of it with your own work.

What is actually in this portfolio

  • Home shows the marketing pitch: a centered hero with a call-to-action that jumps to another tab, a scrolling feature marquee, a card grid, and this blog block.
  • Showcase shows the same building blocks wearing their four art directions: default, cutie, editorial, and riso. Same data, four personalities.
  • Guide covers real instructions for editing, publishing, and replacing this demo.
  • Playground shows the custom HTML block doing things the other blocks cannot, with custom CSS and a video embed.

Under the hood you are looking at: five skin options with token-driven motion, per-block design pickers, a reusable card library (one edit propagates everywhere), drag-and-drop ordering, undo and redo, a media vault, a full blog engine, and view scale control. The Guide tab walks through all of it.

Know the limits

The platform is honest about what it is not (yet):

  • Mobile is untested. Everything renders, but serious editing wants a desktop.
  • Last save wins. Two devices editing the same hosted portfolio means no merge. The newest Save replaces everything.
  • Images do not migrate. Export and import moves content, not image bytes. Externally hosted image URLs are the safe form.
  • Auth is a guardrail. The self-hosted password gate stops accidents, not attackers.

Make it yours

Open the editor, drag things around, change the words, and export the result. Nothing here is precious: the demo exists to be deleted.

  • Press Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + E to enter edit mode, or open with ?edit=true.
  • Open the editor and try changing a card name in step 6, then come back here to see the cascade.
  • Export the JSON when you are happy, and replace content/portfolio.json in your fork (or import it into a hosted account from the dashboard).

Welcome. The keyboard is yours.

posts.title: How to build a portfolio here
posts.content:
A practical recipe, from empty fork to published site, plus the fine print worth knowing before you start.

1. Get the code running

Fork the repository, run npm install and npm run dev, and open localhost:3000. That is the whole setup. The editor works with zero configuration.

2. Enter edit mode

Visit with ?edit=true or press Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + E. You get the block editor, the hidden Posts and Site tabs, and undo and redo history.

3. Fill in your content

Add a hero, an app grid, an entry list, a marquee. Give each block its own art direction. The four designs are siblings, so the same data renders four different ways. Reorder by dragging, duplicate cards from the library, set skins, accent color, font, and view scale in Site settings.

4. Publish (the fork path)

Press Export in the editor toolbar, open the downloaded JSON, and copy-paste its contents over content/portfolio.json in your repo. Do not gitignore public/uploads, as this serves as your local library image hub, then git push. The rebuild is the publish. The site bakes the document at build time.

5. Or go hosted

Deploy with the Vercel checklist in the README (Firebase + Cloudflare KV + R2), sign up from the hub, onboard, and press Save. Visitors get your work at /u/your-name immediately, no rebuilds. The export and import bridge moves an existing portfolio between the two worlds; just remember it carries content, not image bytes.

The fine print

  • Editing is desktop-first. Mobile renders but is untested for real work.
  • Hosted saves are last-save-wins. One editor at a time is the safe assumption.
  • The self-hosted password gate is a guardrail, not security. Hosted accounts use real Firebase auth.
  • If something breaks, open an issue on the repository. A lot of this is young and untested, and reports directly shape the roadmap.

posts.title: Why four art directions
posts.content:
Art direction, not a different product. The four designs (default, cutie, editorial, riso) live alongside each other in the same block, same schema, same editor. Per block. You set a direction on the hero, the marquee, the entry list, the grid. Some portfolios are editorial through and through; others flip per section. Both are fine.

The trade-off, plain

Without art direction you have one design. With art direction you have four, and the design picker is one click. The cost is per-block work, not a new product.

How to pick

  • Default for portfolios that need to read as professional without distraction. Calm borders, mono URL fields, lift on hover.
  • Cutie for portfolios that lean into craft. Polaroid frames, washi tape, candy tags. The kinder art direction.
  • Editorial for portfolios that are about the writing. Numbered rows, hairline rules, serif-italic titles. The thinking person.
  • Riso for portfolios that are loud on purpose. Two-color misprint ink, halftone fields, FIG. captions. The poster print.

How it works under the hood

Each block has a design field, an enum of four values. The renderer dispatches the value to one of four thin components, all wrapping a shared skeleton. The decoration lives in globals.css under .dsn-cutie, .dsn-editorial, and .dsn-riso; the colors flow through the skin tokens so every design stays on-brand across the three skins.

posts.title: What local-first means here
posts.content:
The entire portfolio is one JSON document in localStorage. That is the truth of the platform. Every mutation you make writes to that one key; the editor reads it back, the renderer reads it back, the hosted mirror reads it back. There is no database in the B path. There is one key in a cloud bucket in the A path.

Why this is the right shape

  • It is fast. There is no network hop for editing, and the editor is offline-first by accident.
  • It is portable. One file in, one file out. Export, import, hand it to a friend.
  • It is honest. The document is the source of truth; the storage engine is swappable.

What this means for you

Your work is always exportable. Cloud or no cloud, the file is yours. The hosted path adds a Save button, a share link, and a way for visitors to view without an account. The fork path keeps the file in content/portfolio.json, baked at build time.

The honest limits

Local-first means the fork path is fully yours. The hosted path is a different contract: a Save pushes to a cloud bucket, a refresh reads the latest version. Last save wins on the cloud. Two devices editing the same portfolio will overwrite each other. That is a deliberate MVP limit, not a bug.
